system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 9 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2193-11-01 22:07:00 to 2193-11-10 19:38:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease, type 1 diabetes, and a mechanical heart valve was admitted for evaluation and treatment of a non-healing left foot ulcer with dry gangrene. She underwent a diagnostic left lower extremity angiogram, which revealed a near-occlusive lesion in the left superficial femoral artery. She remained hemodynamically stable throughout her stay, with no complications from the procedure. IV vancomycin was continued for infection prophylaxis, and anticoagulation was managed with a heparin drip that was discontinued once her INR reached a therapeutic level of 3.1. She was discharged home with instructions to continue oral medications, receive IV vancomycin on dialysis days, and follow up for a scheduled left femoral endarterectomy. The patient tolerated a regular diet, ambulated independently, and had stable vital signs at discharge.
problems: Atherosclerosis of native arteries of the extremities with gangrene
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Coronary atherosclerosis of unspecified type of vessel, native or graft
Heart valve replaced by other means

Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted with left foot ulcers and you underwent a left 
femoral endarterectomy and patch angioplasty.  You are now ready 
to complete your recovery at home.  Please follow the 
instructions below: 

WHAT TO EXPECT:
1. It is normal to feel tired, this will last for ___ weeks 
You should get up out of bed every day and gradually increase 
your activity each day 
Unless you were told not to bear any weight on operative foot: 
you may walk and you may go up and down stairs 
Increase your activities as you can tolerate- do not do too 
much right away!
2. It is normal to have swelling of the leg you were operated 
on:
Elevate your leg above the level of your heart (use ___ 
pillows or a recliner) every ___ hours throughout the day and at 
night
Avoid prolonged periods of standing or sitting without your 
legs elevated
3. It is normal to have a decreased appetite, your appetite will 
return with time 
You will probably lose your taste for food and lose some 
weight 
Eat small frequent meals
It is important to eat nutritious food options (high fiber, 
lean meats, vegetables/fruits, low fat, low cholesterol) to 
maintain your strength and assist in wound healing
To avoid constipation: eat a high fiber diet and use stool 
softener while taking pain medication

MEDICATION:
Take aspirin as instructed 
Follow your discharge medication instructions

ACTIVITIES:
No driving until post-op visit and you are no longer taking 
pain medications
Unless you were told not to bear any weight on operative foot: 

You should get up every day, get dressed and walk
You should gradually increase your activity
You may up and down stairs, go outside and/or ride in a car
Increase your activities as you can tolerate- do not do too 
much right away!
No heavy lifting, pushing or pulling (greater than 5 pounds) 
until your post op visit 
You may shower (unless you have stitches or foot incisions) no 
direct spray on incision, let the soapy water run over incision, 
rinse and pat dry
Your incision may be left uncovered, unless you have small 
amounts of drainage from the wound, then place a dry dressing 
over the area that is draining, as needed

CALL THE OFFICE FOR: ___
Redness that extends away from your incision
A sudden increase in pain that is not controlled with pain 
medication
A sudden change in the ability to move or use your leg or the 
ability to feel your leg
Temperature greater than 100.5F for 24 hours
Bleeding, new or increased drainage from incision or white, 
yellow or green drainage from incisions

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the vascular surgery team. You've been admitted tonight because of the ulcers on your left foot and the blockage we saw in your leg artery last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I remember. The angiogram showed a bad blockage in my left leg, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It's a near-occlusive lesion in the left superficial femoral artery. We’re planning to fix that with a procedure called an endarterectomy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that like a bypass? I thought I was getting a bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We initially planned a bypass using your own vein, but we need to check first if the vein is usable. That’s why we’re doing a vein mapping ultrasound tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. And what about my blood thinner? I’m on Coumadin for my mechanical valve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We’re stopping your Coumadin for now and starting a heparin drip. That’s safer around surgery. We’ll restart Coumadin after the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the heparin will be adjusted based on my blood tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll monitor your PTT and adjust the drip to keep it in the right range. Once your INR is back up to 3.0–3.5, we’ll stop the heparin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll need dialysis too—usually on Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve scheduled dialysis for tomorrow. The transplant nephrology team will be following you as well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your vein mapping ultrasound was done this morning. The greater saphenous vein in your left leg is patent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So we can use it for the bypass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll find out during surgery. Sometimes that vein was used in prior heart surgery and might not be available.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a CABG years ago—could they have taken it then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. If it was harvested, we’ll have to use a different approach. But we have a backup plan—endarterectomy with patch angioplasty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, as long as the blood flow gets fixed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished dialysis. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little tired, but okay. No cramps this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep monitoring your labs, especially potassium and fluid status.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning your surgery for tomorrow morning. Any questions before then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just—what exactly is an endarterectomy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We open the artery and remove the plaque buildup. Then we sew in a patch to keep it open. It’s a direct way to fix the blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll be in the ICU after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the VICU for one night, just to monitor your heart and circulation closely, given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you're back from surgery. The procedure went well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did you use my vein for the bypass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We explored the greater saphenous vein, but it was tied off—likely used in your prior CABG. So instead, we did a femoral endarterectomy with patch angioplasty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that as good as a bypass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For your type of blockage, yes. It restores blood flow and should help your foot ulcers heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m glad it’s done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.8. We’re still running the heparin drip but getting close to stopping it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will I be back on Coumadin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re already on it—4 mg daily. Once your INR hits 3.0–3.5 and stays there, we’ll stop the heparin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—am I back on all of them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, including tacrolimus, sirolimus, and aspirin. The transplant team reviewed everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The podiatry team cultured your foot ulcer today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was there an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The culture grew coagulase-negative staph. It’s a common skin bacterium, but we’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need different antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. You’re already on IV vancomycin on dialysis days, which covers it. We’ll continue that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your INR is now 3.9.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that too high?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s slightly above our target of 3.0–3.5, but since we’re stopping the heparin today, it should stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. Can I start walking more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the physical therapist saw you today. You’re doing well. They recommend home physical therapy after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need help at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, home nursing and physical therapy. You’ll need help with wound checks and mobility at first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re healing well. The incision looks clean, no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my foot ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Podiatry says it’s stable. Improved blood flow should help it heal over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on a special diet too, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 2 grams sodium and 2 grams potassium. It’s important for your heart and kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep that up at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you have fever over 100.5, increased pain, redness spreading from the incision, or drainage that’s yellow or green.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And activity?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can walk and go up and down stairs, but no heavy lifting—nothing over five pounds—for two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I shower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, let water run over the incision, pat dry. No soaking in a tub yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. We’ve arranged home nursing, physical therapy, and your follow-up with Dr. Patel in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I keep taking Coumadin, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 4 mg daily. Continue all your other meds too—especially the transplant and dialysis ones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home today. The team is proud of your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember: elevate your leg when sitting, eat small frequent meals, and keep up with your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And call if anything seems off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your incision can stay uncovered unless there’s drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Just a dry dressing if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest well and keep building your strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with end-stage renal disease, a history of pancreas and kidney transplants, and a mechanical heart valve was readmitted for treatment of left foot ulcers and a significant blockage in the left superficial femoral artery. She underwent vein mapping, which showed a patent greater saphenous vein, but during surgery, it was found to be tied off, likely from a prior CABG. As a result, she had a left femoral endarterectomy with patch angioplasty instead of a bypass. She was managed postoperatively in the VICU, transitioned from heparin to Coumadin, and maintained on her home immunosuppressive and dialysis regimen. Cultures from her foot ulcer grew coagulase-negative staph, but no treatment change was needed. She worked with physical therapy, was deemed safe for discharge home with home health services, and was given detailed wound care and activity instructions. Her INR was therapeutic at discharge, and she was scheduled for follow-up in two weeks.
